source.title: Elucidating Meta-Structures of Noisy Labels in Semantic Segmentation by Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Yao-Ru Luo; Guo-Shuai Liu; Yuanhao Guo; Ge Yang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some equations and table entries are garbled in the supplied text; those results are not reconstructed where the layout is unclear.
record.tranche_reason: Tests noisy-label learning in semantic segmentation with pixel-level label corruption, rather than the original classification setup. It reports segmentation performance and learning curves, not the original study’s training-error and test-error measures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports pixel-level random-label training loss and test Dice curves, but the curves are figure-only. Results cited from Zhang et al. (2021) and Arpit et al. (2017) are not extracted as this paper’s results. The paper does not report a direct fit of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
record.test_reason: The study extends noisy-label experiments to semantic segmentation. Its own learning curves bear on V6, and its corruption experiments test V4's predicted degradation. Random-label training loss is also examined, but does not establish V1's near-zero training error.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that segmentation networks learn spatial meta-structures retained in noisy labels, with degradation when those structures are perturbed or removed. They interpret early high test scores followed by collapse under random labels as patterns-before-memorization behavior. Their interpretation does not establish zero training error or directly measure individual-label memorization.
record.recipe_differences: Studies pixel-level label corruption in semantic segmentation using U-Net and DeepLabv3+, with SGD and cross-entropy stated for the main experiments; it does not reproduce the original classification setup or its training/test error measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance changes with the noise transition matrix rank and complete randomization distance; random-label training loss is reported to converge more quickly at higher generation probability.

fits_no_version.finding: RL with approximately 31% pixel-label error produces worse segmentation than RCL with 49% error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Segmentation generalization depends on retained spatial semantic structure, beyond the fraction of correctly labeled pixels.

fits_no_version.finding: Training loss converges faster as random foreground-generation probability increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimization dynamics under independent random pixel labels depend on their foreground-generation probability.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are given for the relevant noisy-label results. Random-label learning curves are figure-only without numerical values. The paper reports segmentation Dice/IoU, not training error or test error at chance, and the supplied Table 5 class-pair annotations are partly garbled.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 has flattened condition/value associations that cannot be reliably reconstructed from the supplied text. Table 6 concerns perturbed object boundaries, which are not named by the claim versions. Table 8 concerns dynamic full-rank RCL and is not a direct test of the listed versions.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error, a chance-calibrated test result, and a documented unchanged hyperparameter comparison between clean and completely random labels are not established.
The small training-time factor relative to true labels and convergence time across corrupted-label fractions are not tested. Foreground-generation probability is a different manipulation.
No fitting experiments on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit throughout corruption, a full scalar corruption-fraction sweep, and a calibrated chance endpoint are not established.
No controlled comparison of weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation, including their removal on true labels.
No direct measurement separates acquisition of shared patterns from memorization of individual noisy labels; the learning-order inference rests on test-performance dynamics.

missing.what: Six Cityscapes-3 RCL results are omitted: sampling probabilities 0.2, 0.4, and 0.8 give IoU 94.3, 94.1, and 93.7; flipping probabilities 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8 give 93.8, 93.4, and 93.1, against clean 94.3.
A third full-rank Cityscapes-3 condition has minimum CRD 0.2 and IoU 92.7 against clean 94.3.
The authors explicitly report similar random-label learning dynamics for DeepLabv3+. The supplied text references supplementary results without providing their curves or conditions.
missing.locator: Section 5.2, reference to Supplementary Material B.2

record.verdict_notes: No V1 verdict is warranted from an unspecified loss plateau or an uncalibrated low test Dice score. Missing measurements are untested components, not evidence against V1. Table 4 and dynamic-RCL Table 8 were explicitly declared left out, so they are not listed as missing. The supplied text's binary 0.5-flipping result is internally inconsistent with its complete-randomization account and needs source clarification.

versions.untested_parts: Tests independent random pixel labels in semantic segmentation, but does not state zero or near-zero training error, test error at chance, or whether architecture and training hyperparameters were unchanged from the original sources.
No comparison of training time or convergence time against true labels, and no convergence-time sweep over corrupted-label fractions.
Does not train on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Tests several pixel-label randomization conditions and reports test segmentation scores, but does not establish perfect training fit or a steady rise in test error toward chance as corruption increases. Random labels are separately examined in a figure-only learning curve.
Does not test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation as factors in fitting random labels or generalizing on true labels.

Tests whether learning patterns precedes memorization for random pixel labels in segmentation. Does not compare a quantified real-label learning phase with a quantified random-label learning phase or test the full claim across models and datasets.

rows.subject: U-Net
rows.operation_detail: Trained on ER images with random pixel labels; the paper varies the probability of assigning foreground labels.
rows.value: Figure only; text says Dice scores fluctuate substantially and reach several high values in the first stage, then drop quickly and converge to a low value.
rows.note: The text interprets the early high Dice scores as a period before the network is strongly influenced by random labels; it does not give exact values or say the training error reaches zero.
rows.check: The early high test-Dice values followed by collapse support the authors' qualitative patterns-before-memorization interpretation. They do not establish V1's training-fit or chance-performance endpoints. Generation probability zero is a constant-label control, not a nondegenerate random labeling.

rows.value: Figure only; text says loss converges more quickly under a higher generation probability.
rows.note: The text describes faster convergence as indicating a higher tendency to memorize random labels, but gives no exact training loss or training error.
rows.check: Convergence to an unspecified constant loss does not establish zero or near-zero training error. Faster convergence across foreground-generation probabilities measures neither V6's learning order nor V2's comparison with true-label training.

relationships.condition: DeepLabv3+ on Cityscapes-3 with different noise transition matrix ranks
relationships.reason: R22-R29 show near-clean performance for full-rank corruption, sharp losses when class distinctions disappear, and one-class predictions under rank-1 corruption. This qualifies a smooth degradation account by the structure of corruption; it does not establish perfect training fit.
relationships.display_finding: Full-rank corruption preserved near-clean performance, while losing class distinctions caused sharp losses and rank-1 corruption produced one-class predictions.
